conversation.content:
Good morning—I’m so glad you’re here. I’m Claire, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and help you feel supported as you settle into new motherhood.

Today I’ll be using a short screening tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s just 10 gentle questions that ask how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to understand your experience so we can offer the best support possible.

Everything you share stays confidential within our care team. We’ll move at your pace, and if any question feels difficult, we can pause or come back to it.

Are you comfortable for us to begin?

First, I’d love to know: in the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—whether about the baby, life, or anything else?
Yes, I have—just yesterday my partner made a silly face while changing the baby’s diaper and I actually giggled. It felt good; I’d say I laugh pretty much the same as I always did.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Most of the time—yeah, I still find things funny. Like yesterday, the baby let out this huge burp right as my mom was giving me advice, and we all just cracked up. I wouldn’t say every single moment, but definitely more yes than no.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Yes, I still look forward to stuff. I’m excited for our weekly coffee date with my moms-group on Thursday, and I’m planning a little outing to the farmer’s market this weekend. I guess I’d say “most of the time”—there are tired moments, but overall I’m still eager for the little things.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really—maybe once or twice I thought, “Should I have burped her longer?” but I don’t dwell on it. I’d say “no, not very often.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason
Sometimes—like in the middle of the night I’ll suddenly worry that her breathing sounds different, even though she’s fine. It’s not every day, but I’d say “yes, occasionally.”
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t felt that way—no panic or real fear. Just the little worries every now and then, but nothing that feels scary.
Things have been getting on top of me
No, most days I keep things pretty steady. There are moments when the laundry piles up or she won’t settle, but I handle it and move on.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, that hasn’t happened. Once I’m in bed I fall asleep pretty easily—actually, the baby’s longer stretch of sleep has been a nice surprise.
I have felt sad or miserable
Hardly at all—maybe just a quick wave of blues one afternoon when I was extra tired, but it passed pretty fast. Overall I’d say “no.”
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t cried at all this week—maybe felt a little teary-eyed once, but no actual tears.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. That hasn’t crossed my mind.

It sounds as though you're navigating early motherhood with resilience and a welcome sense of humor, still laughing with family over the baby's funny moments and planning coffee dates and outings that you genuinely look forward to. You shared that occasional nighttime worries pop up about the baby's breathing, but they pass quickly and haven't escalated into panic or persistent sadness; you're coping well, sleeping when you can, and have not felt overwhelmed, tearful, or hopeless.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 3, Risk Level: Depression not likely (concerns include <sym>Patient explicitly describes recurring, unprompted nighttime worries about breathing, qualifying as "sometimes" anxious without cause.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items are scored 0-3; a total ≤8 suggests <med>postpartum depression</med> is unlikely. Your score of 3 falls well below this threshold. You endorsed only mild, situational <sym>anxiety</sym> (Q4=2) with no persistent low mood, anhedonia, guilt, sleep-mood disruption, or self-harm thoughts. These results do not meet <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, which require ≥5 symptoms (including depressed mood or loss of interest) for two weeks, nor do they indicate an <med>anxiety disorder</med> at this time. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Continue routine postpartum care and re-screen with EPDS at the six-week visit or sooner if mood or anxiety worsens
2. Practice brief relaxation techniques (slow breathing, progressive muscle relaxation) when occasional worries arise
3. Maintain social connections such as your weekly moms-group; consider sharing nighttime worries there for peer reassurance
4. Keep basic self-care priorities-sleep when baby sleeps, balanced snacks, hydration, and gentle walks
5. Seek prompt re-evaluation if you notice persistent sadness, panic episodes, intrusive thoughts, or thoughts of self-harm
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
